headline: Wild Rice Greens Up on Great Island — River Bass Hold Deep as Fluke Push Into the Lower Stretch
subhead: With the shad run six weeks behind us, the river's summer residents are settling into their July pattern — stripers in the cool seams, fluke on the sand, and the first push of blues at the mouth.
body_markdown:
The wild rice is up to my knees along the Great Island flats now, and the pickerelweed's gone purple in every quiet cove from Lord Cove to the Lieutenant River. That's how I mark the calendar this time of year — not by the tide book, though I keep that close too, but by what's blooming in the marsh. Fifty springs of watching this river teaches you that the plants don't lie. When the rice greens up like this, the shad run is a memory, the ospreys are feeding fledglings off the nest platforms at Great Island, and the river settles into its long, hot middle age. That's where we are.

This isn't shad water anymore — that run came and went back in May, right on schedule, and I said my goodbyes to it weeks ago. What we've got now is the river's summer program: striped bass holding in the current seams, the first real push of summer flounder into the lower stretch, white perch working the coves, and bluefish starting to show where the river dumps into the Sound. I flagged this pattern last week — said the bass would stay in the river right through the heat and that fluke would start pushing up from the Sound side. Both of those calls are holding up on the water this week.

The Sound itself is carrying a real thermal gradient right now, cooler out toward New London, warmer up around the western reaches, and that gradient matters for how fish stage at our river mouth. The Connecticut River, even with all that fresh water dumping through, warms up fast in the shallow coves under a July sun — I've felt water in the upper 70s in the skinny stuff off Calves Island by mid-afternoon. That pushes the stripers to look for moving, oxygenated water, and they're finding it in the tidal current off Saybrook Point, under the railroad bridge in Old Saybrook, and around the drawbridge pilings up in Essex. Early light and the last two hours of the incoming are still your best windows before the sun really starts cooking the flats.

At Saybrook Point, the breakwater has been holding fish right at first light — schoolie-to-mid-twenties stripers working bunker pods that push in and out with the tide. Topwater plugs, a Doc or a Gibbs pencil worked with a walk-the-dog retrieve, have drawn some violent strikes right in the white water off the rocks. Once the sun's up and that bite shuts down, guys are switching to bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce, tipped with a curl-tail grub, worked slow along the bottom where the current pinches around the jetty rocks.

Up around Nott Island and the flats off Great Island, the pattern's more subtle — bass tailing in the shallows on the last hour of the flood, working grass shrimp and mummichogs out of the marsh grass. A weightless soft plastic, something like a Slug-Go in white or bone, cast just ahead of a push or a nervous swirl, has been the right call there. It's sight-fishing more than blind-casting, and you need calm water and decent light to see the fish before you cast to them. Mornings with a light southerly have been kinder to that game than the choppier afternoons.

The fluke news is the real story developing right now. We've been seeing keeper-class summer flounder showing up in the deeper channel water off Nott Island and around the Calves Island humps, in fifteen to twenty-two feet, on the tail end of the outgoing tide when the current really gets moving through there. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, have taken fish to four and five pounds. It's not a wide-open bite — you're covering water and picking off fish here and there rather than filling a cooler — but the presence of quality fluke this far up the river, past Essex, is worth noting. That's new water for a lot of guys who only think fluke when they're down in the Sound proper.

White perch are doing what white perch do in July — holding in the deeper holes of the quieter coves, North Cove in Old Lyme and the mouth of the Lieutenant River among them, and they'll take a small piece of nightcrawler or bloodworm fished on a light Carolina rig right along bottom. Not glamorous fishing, but it's steady, and it's a good way to keep kids interested when the bigger bite is slow.

Bluefish are the wildcard piece right now. We're starting to see the first schools working bunker right at the river mouth, out past the Saybrook breakwater toward the Sound, chopping bait on the surface in the mornings. If that bunker migration keeps pushing the way it has along the coast, I'd expect those blues to keep showing here through the next couple weeks, and they'll mix right in with the striper bite on the same tides and the same metal — a one-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins will draw both species out there.

Looking ahead, we're sliding into the first-quarter neap around the 21st, which will soften the current through the river mouth rips for a few days. That usually widens the productive window beyond just the peak of the tide — worth remembering if you can only get out mid-morning rather than at first light. If the heat holds and the coves keep climbing into the upper 70s, I'd expect the bass to keep favoring the moving water under the bridges and around the breakwater rather than the open flats during the day, saving the shallow work for dawn and dusk. The fluke push is the one to watch — if it keeps building the way it has this week, the lower river could have a real summer flounder fishery worth targeting through August.
